Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i went back to alder hollow in late october to finish a woodland map i had started in spring. the county had asked for a map of paths, wet ground, and the old stone boundary, not a survey of every tree. i knew that on paper, but once i was there with the notebook open i kept wanting to record more. the morning was cool, and the leaves were still holding water from rain the night before. my paper map had softened at one corner where it had sat against my flask.

i began at the north gate, where the public footpath comes in beside a leaning ash. in spring i had marked the gate as being about twelve metres east of the stream crossing. this time my tape measure and the map did not agree, so i checked the crossing from both banks and found that i had used the bend in the stream, rather than the narrow plank bridge, as my reference point. i changed the note, though i did not redraw the whole path until i had walked it again. the difference was small on the ground but clear enough to matter on the map.

there were three kinds of ground that i was trying to distinguish: firm leaf litter, soft soil that held a boot print, and patches where water stayed on the surface. i used a short line of blue pencil for the last kind, rather than filling the spaces in, because the puddles were broken up by roots and leaves. at one point i wrote “wet” beside a patch of bracken and then paused, since wet could mean the leaves were damp, not that the ground itself was holding water. i changed it to “standing water under bracken.” that was longer, but it said what i had actually seen.

near the old boundary stones, i had another problem. the stones did not make a straight line, and two of them were almost hidden under hazel branches. i followed the line slowly, marking each visible stone with a small cross and leaving gaps where i could not see the next one. my first draft connected the gaps with a smooth line, which made the boundary look more certain than it was. i erased that section and put short dashes instead. a walker looking at the map might prefer one clear line, but i did not want to imply that i had seen stones where there were only leaves and guesses.

1. things i checked before moving on
- the footpath was still open at the north gate
- the narrow plank bridge was firm underfoot, although its left edge had moss on it
- the stream crossed the path in one shallow channel, not the two channels shown on my spring sketch
- the old boundary stones were visible at four points, with no clear view between the second and third

at the southern end of the hollow, i noticed a faint track that was not on my first map. it ran from a fallen birch toward a patch of holly, then disappeared into leaf cover. i walked along it for about thirty paces, but i could not tell whether it was used regularly or only made by animals moving through the undergrowth. i did not label it as a path. in my notes i called it a possible track and added the date, because i did not want a later reader to confuse my observation with a settled route.

i had expected to finish the map before lunch, but i spent longer checking the stream and the boundary than i planned. the light also changed under the trees, and some of the pale marks on my draft were hard to see. when i stopped by the fallen birch, i ate an apple and compared the notebook with the map. i found that i had copied the number for one marker incorrectly. the notebook said 17, while the map said 71. i corrected it there, and checked the other numbered marks as well. none of them needed changing.

on the way back, i met a woman walking a small brown dog. she asked whether the track near the holly went through to the lane. i said i did not know, and that i had only followed it a short distance. she replied, “it looks like it might, but it gets lost every autumn.” i wrote that down afterward, not as confirmation that the track reached the lane, but as something a local walker had told me. her wording seemed useful because it described the uncertainty without making the route sound definite.

when i got home, i laid the damp map flat between two sheets of unprinted paper. i transferred the corrected bridge reference, the broken blue marks for standing water, and the dashed boundary section onto a clean copy. i left the faint track as a dotted line ending near the holly, with “possible track; extent unclear” beside it. i also kept the note about the dog walker separate from the map symbols, since it was information from a conversation, not something i had verified in the hollow. the finished page was less tidy than the version i had first imagined, but it matched what i had actually been able to see.", "output": "I went back to Alder Hollow in late October to finish a woodland map I had started in spring. The county had asked for a map of paths, wet ground, and the old stone boundary, not a survey of every tree. I knew that on paper, but once I was there with my notebook open, I kept wanting to record more. The morning was cool, and the leaves were still holding water from the rain the night before. One corner of my paper map had softened where it had rested against my flask.

I began at the north gate, where the public footpath enters beside a leaning ash. In spring, I had marked the gate as about twelve metres east of the stream crossing. This time, my tape measure and the map did not agree, so I checked the crossing from both banks. I found that I had used the bend in the stream, rather than the narrow plank bridge, as my reference point. I changed the note, though I waited to redraw the whole path until I had walked it again. The difference was small on the ground, but clear enough to matter on the map.

I was trying to distinguish three kinds of ground: firm leaf litter, soft soil that held a boot print, and patches where water stayed on the surface. I used a short blue-pencil line for the last kind rather than filling in the spaces, because roots and leaves broke up the puddles. At one point, I wrote “wet” beside a patch of bracken, then paused. Wet could mean that the leaves were damp, not that the ground itself was holding water. I changed the note to “standing water under bracken.” It was longer, but it said what I had actually seen.

Near the old boundary stones, I ran into another problem. The stones did not form a straight line, and two were almost hidden beneath hazel branches. I followed the line slowly, marking each visible stone with a small cross and leaving gaps where I could not see the next one. In my first draft, I had connected the gaps with a smooth line, making the boundary look more certain than it was. I erased that section and used short dashes instead. A walker looking at the map might prefer one clear line, but I did not want to suggest that I had seen stones where there were only leaves and guesses.

1. Things I checked before moving on
- The footpath was still open at the north gate.
- The narrow plank bridge was firm underfoot, although its left edge was mossy.
- The stream crossed the path in one shallow channel, not the two channels shown on my spring sketch.
- I could see the old boundary stones at four points, with no clear view between the second and third.

At the southern end of the hollow, I noticed a faint track that was not on my first map. It ran from a fallen birch toward a patch of holly, then disappeared beneath the leaves. I followed it for about thirty paces, but could not tell whether people used it regularly or whether animals had simply made it through the undergrowth. I did not label it as a path. In my notes, I called it a possible track and added the date so a later reader would not confuse my observation with an established route.

I had expected to finish the map before lunch, but I spent longer checking the stream and the boundary than I had planned. The light also changed beneath the trees, making some of the pale marks on my draft hard to see. When I stopped by the fallen birch, I ate an apple and compared my notebook with the map. I found that I had copied one marker’s number incorrectly: the notebook said 17, while the map said 71. I corrected it and checked the other numbered marks as well. None of them needed changing.

On the way back, I met a woman walking a small brown dog. She asked whether the track near the holly went through to the lane. I said I did not know and had followed it only a short distance. She replied, “It looks like it might, but it gets lost every autumn.” I wrote that down afterward—not as confirmation that the track reached the lane, but as something a local walker had told me. Her wording seemed useful because it described the uncertainty without making the route sound definite.

When I got home, I laid the damp map flat between two sheets of unprinted paper. I transferred the corrected bridge reference, the broken blue marks for standing water, and the dashed boundary section onto a clean copy. I left the faint track as a dotted line ending near the holly, with “possible track; extent unclear” beside it. I also kept the dog walker’s comment separate from the map symbols, since it came from a conversation and was not something I had verified in the hollow. we met at the old forestry gate at 8:20. there were seven of us, including coordinator Jo Bell and a botanist called Nikhil Rao. jo started with a safety talk and pointed out that the eastern ditch had deep water after the previous night's rain. she also said we should not try to cross it just to keep a straight transect. that was useful advice, because the map showed a short route there that looked easy from the gate. we split into two teams, and my group took the north loop, beginning beside a stand of silver birch. the first ten minutes went slowly while we checked that the phone location and paper grid were close to each other.

The app was good at recording a line once it had settled, though the first location mark wandered about six metres while we stood still. we waited a little and used the paper map to check where we were, instead of drawing the line from the first reading. mossline lets you add a point, a line, or a polygon, and each can have a short note and a photo. it was fairly easy to learn, but the icons for point and line were similar in the shade. i chose a line when i meant to add a point at a fallen oak, then deleted it and entered the feature again. the app did not lose the note when i corrected the geometry, which saved some fiddling.

1. What worked in the field

The best part of the method was the shared naming system. before we walked, jo handed out a one-page list with codes for broad habitat types, path condition, and visible water. “Use the code first, then add what you can actually see,” she said. That kept our notes consistent without making every patch sound identical. At the western edge, we recorded a narrow strip of wet ground as W2, then added that the sedges were ankle-high and the surface had soft hollows. I liked that the code did not force us to pretend we knew the exact plant community. Nikhil checked one patch and said, “We can call this sedge-rich for now; I wouldn’t name a species from this distance.” That was a helpful limit, not a weakness.

There were some annoying practical details. the borrowed phone was in a thick waterproof case, and the side button was hard to press with gloves on. the screen was readable outside if i turned the brightness up, but that used battery faster. by lunch it was down to 41 percent, even though i had started at full charge. jo had brought two power banks, so it was not a crisis, but the app has no obvious low-power setting. I also found that the photo captions were easy to miss in the small preview. I took a picture of a broken culvert and only noticed later that the caption field was blank. I added it while we were sitting at the picnic table, where the phone had a stronger signal.

That signal was inconsistent in the northern hollow. the map tiles loaded before we left the gate, as jo recommended, but the base map labels went pale and the small stream was difficult to distinguish from a contour line. our paper copy was better for seeing the whole route, while the phone was better for attaching a precise observation. i ended up using both, which was not a problem, although carrying the clipboard along the bramble section was awkward. The paper sheet also got damp at the lower corner. It stayed readable, but a plastic sleeve would have helped.

The route itself was varied enough to show why a single label for the wood would not have been useful. We passed a broad track with compacted gravel, an old coppice area, a small pond with a timber edge, and several places where fallen branches partly blocked the path. Near the pond, the map showed a viewing bench that had been removed; we marked its old location as a point and noted that no bench was present. I appreciated the option to record that kind of mismatch without changing the base layer. At the southern boundary, brambles covered one of the mapped access gaps, so our group recorded it as obstructed rather than pushing through.

The volunteer briefing was friendly and not overlong, although the first explanation of the habitat codes moved quickly. I asked jo to repeat the difference between “scrub edge” and “young woodland,” and she gave an example from the west side of the pond. After that, I was more confident about choosing a code, but I still checked with Nikhil when a patch was borderline. Nobody treated uncertainty like a mistake. At the end of each section we compared notes, and one of the other volunteers, Mara, said, “It’s better to leave a clear question than to make a tidy guess.” That felt like a good rule for this sort of mapping.

On the second morning, we reviewed our entries in the village hall before going out again. the export screen gave a table with time, category, location, and note, and the points appeared on a simple map. I could not find a way to sort the notes by category on the phone, so Jo used her laptop for that part. Two of our path observations had nearly the same location, because we had stopped at either side of a bend; we kept both, since the surface changed there. We also corrected one label from “open ground” to “clearing,” after looking at the shared code sheet. The edits were saved with the original times visible, which made it easier to remember what we had seen first.

I liked the balance between walking and recording, and the paper backup made the process feel less dependent on a phone signal. The small text in the legend, the battery use, and the fiddly photo captions all slowed me down at points.
